Remediation Recommendations The recommendations for structure replacements to resolve fish passage problems assume that more detailed planning will be done once a site is selected for remedial action. The following steps should be included in the detailed planning: 1. The road users determined as having the ‘road responsibility’ for each crossing structure should review, and correct where needed, that determination. 2. A professional biologist should review each site to determine that there is fish use of the stream at site (where not presently known) and that there is sufficient quantity and quality of accessible upstream fish habitat to justify investing in the site. 3. A professional engineer should survey the site, determine the engineering details of the site, make the final choice of new crossing structure type, and determine the detailed design of the crossing structure. The crossing structure options that are listed are all adequate for fish passage, but the engineer will need to consider additional factors such as fill depth, sight- lines, road width, traffic type and frequency, road corners, and more refined cost estimates. A biologist cannot account for all of these factors, and also the guidelines do not include acquisition of the information needed to address the factors. 4. A professional biologist should then return to the site and develop an Environmental Management Plan for the works. The Plan will confirm the suitability of the engineered design (especially channel width), specify the details of the new channel (substrate size and distribution, pool/riffle design if appropriate, LWD installation, slope, etc.), suggest a plan for minimizing downstream sedimentation during the work, identify any fish salvage requirements during dewatering of the work site, specify the in-stream work timing window for the site, and recommend whether an Environmental Monitor should be on site during the work. If a decision has already been made to have an Environmental Monitor on site, this can be reflected in the Environmental Management Plan by reducing the detail (and therefore time/cost) of the Plan. In such a case the Environmental Monitor can verbally provide the details regarding the precise channel design to the construction crew; however sufficient detail must be in the Plan to allow the construction contractor to accurately estimate costs when bidding on the project. 3.1.2. Structure Risks 1. Bridges The recommended bridge designs for each site include bridge length, bridge width (single, double, or highway), and minimum channel width. The bridge length and width are estimates for use in estimating cost; the professional engineer designing the bridge will determine the actual values. The minimum channel width is intended to provide direction to the engineer to include in his bridge design – it may be increased but should not be decreased without agreement from a professional biologist. The minimum channel width specified for bridges is the stream channel width plus 1-2 meters, to provide a small amount of room for lateral structure in the channel. I suggest that bridge designs include a minimum of 1 – 2 m width of coarse riprap on each side of the channel, at no greater slope than 1:1, between the channel and vertical abutments. This riprap will provide an irregular channel edge with variable but relatively slow current speeds at high 18 flows, assisting upstream fish passage, and reducing the risk of scouring of channel edges immediately downstream from the bridge. Estimated bridge lengths allow for this width of riprap. The risks to fish habitat associated with installation and use of a bridge meeting modern standards are low. Risks for bridges are: Downstream sedimentation during installation – this results from removal of the old culvert and construction of the new channel. In theory this can be completely avoided by diverting all stream flow around the work site, pumping sediment-containing water away from the work site and the stream, and washing the new streambed prior to re-establishing the stream flow. In practice complete elimination of downstream sedimentation may not be feasible without a large additional investment in time and money, which may not be warranted given the low impact on fish habitat of low concentration and short duration sediment release during the in-stream work timing window. Channel diversions may also result in significant sediment production, and significant loss of part of the channel bank and riparian habitats; in confined gullies they may not be possible. Channel construction – the constructed channel may be too narrow (hence I have specified minimum channel widths), the new streambed may lack sufficient fines (resulting in subterranean flow during low water), washout of the newly constructed streambed may occur if the gradient is over a few percent (resulting in high-energy erosion at peak flows), the streambed may lack pool/riffle structure (not applicable where there is significant bedload movement), or the streambed may lack appropriate surface texture (boulders, etc.). With good initial design and input from an Environmental Monitor these problems should be avoidable; without the Environmental Monitor construction crews may or may not be able to “do it right”. Downstream sedimentation after installation – usually limited to sediment inputs from the bridge deck, approaches, and ditches. These risks can be minimized by ensuring that the approaches are well gravelled, the deck has no cracks/holes and is full width, and (preferably) the curbs are solid. Ditches need to be designed to minimize the amount of water that reaches the stream, and should be armoured to prevent erosion. Flood water impacts – abnormally high peak flows can result in scouring of the new channel under the bridge. The significance of such flows can be reduced by sloping riprap back from each side of the channel, separating the channel from the vertical walls of the abutments. This may provide an approximation of a natural floodplain zone, slowing the current speed along the edges of the new channel. In contrast, vertical abutments rising straight up from the channel edges may act in a manner similar to the sides of a culvert, and current speeds will slow very little along the edge of the channels. Bedload and Debris movement – bedload and debris should move unimpeded under a clearspan bridge, especially if the channel is slightly wider than the natural channel and if sloped riprap is present on each side of the channel. Bridges with mid-span supports rising out of the channel may require monitoring for debris jams, and the channel structure may be altered due to changes in erosion and/or deposition processes resulting from the pier. Beaver dams – beaver dams are relatively seldom of concern with bridges, because water flow continues even if the inlet to the channel under the bridge is dammed. If roadbed depth is too shallow or the roadbed material is too fine there may be problems with reduced fill stability due to saturation due to the beaver pond. Where beaver activity is present the construction design and fill type of the bridge approaches should take into account the possibility of ponding on the upstream side. 19 2. Open-bottom Arches The recommended open-bottom arch designs include arch width and length. Arch length was calculated as the length of the existing culvert, plus two metres, because culverts tend to be too short and because the arch is likely to be set lower than the existing culvert outlet. The length could be shortened if the road fill is narrowed (possible at some sites). The arch length and width are estimates for use in estimating cost; the professional engineer designing the arch should determine the actual values. The minimum arch width is intended to provide definitive direction to the engineer to include in his arch design – it may be increased but should not be decreased without agreement from a professional biologist. The minimum width specified for arches is the stream channel width, plus 1-2 meters to provide a small amount of room for lateral structure in the channel, plus 2 metres to allow for 1 m of riprap on each side of the channel. Arch designs should include a minimum of 1 m of coarse riprap on each side of the channel, between the channel and the vertical arch wall. This riprap provides an irregular channel edge with variable but relatively slow current speeds at high flows, assists upstream fish passage and reduces the risk of scouring under the sides of the arch where concrete footings are not used. Highway arches normally have concrete footings; industrial road arches frequently do not have such footings. Estimated arch widths allow for this width of riprap. Site 2006.621 is an example where the effective width of the arch has been reduced by half by armouring. Open-bottom arches are the next preferred option to bridges for all fish stream crossings; the risks to fish habitat associated with installation and use of a properly sized and installed arch are reasonably low. Risks for arches are: Downstream sedimentation during installation – as for bridges, except if concrete footings are used there will be a prolonged installation period. Channel construction – as for bridges. Downstream sedimentation after installation – as for bridges. However, the full road width will be present over the crossing site, rather than the narrowed width typical of bridges other than highway bridges. Hence road surface sediment inputs are less likely to occur with an open-bottom arch than for a bridge, unless the new road fill has not been properly compacted. Flood water impacts – The significance of abnormally high flows can be minimized by sloping riprap back from each side of the channel, separating the channel from the vertical walls of the arch. This also helps to prevent erosion under the sides of arches that do not have concrete footings. As for bridges, this may provide an approximation of a natural floodplain zone, slowing the current speed along the edges of the new channel. Bedload and Debris movement – bedload and debris can more easily accumulate in an open- bottom arch than under a bridge, and cleaning out the bedload or debris is more difficult. Therefore arches were not recommended for sites with high bedload or debris movement. Beaver dams – beavers will base their dams on any structure that narrows the channel, or otherwise makes their dam construction more efficient. The inlet of an open-bottom arch is such a location. The smallest open-bottom arch recommended is a 3 m width, which allows for a 1 m channel width plus 1 m of riprap on each side of the channel to protect the base of the arch. This width will automatically result in a height that will seldom be entirely blocked by a beaver dam, allowing water to continue flowing and making a road washout unlikely. 20 3. Embedded Culverts Embedded culverts were recommended only for streams with marginal habitat value, and only where there was no existing beaver activity. The recommended embedded culvert design included culvert width and culvert length. Culvert length was calculated as the length of the existing culvert, plus two metres because culverts tend to be too short and because the embedded culvert is likely to be set lower than the existing culvert outlet. The length could be shortened if the road fill is narrowed, which may be possible at some sites. The culvert length and width are estimates for use in estimating cost; the professional engineer designing the embedded culvert should determine the actual values. The minimum culvert width is intended to provide direction to the engineer to include in his culvert design – it may be increased but should not be decreased without agreement from a professional biologist. The minimum channel width specified for embedded culverts is the stream channel width plus 1-2 meters, to provide a small amount of room for lateral structure in the channel. Embedded culverts have the highest risks of the three primary categories of crossing structures, and therefore are restricted to streams with marginal fish habitat value. Embedded culverts are only recommended for sites where they can be less than 30 m in length, consistent with Robison (2006). Risks for embedded culverts are: Downstream sedimentation during installation – as for bridges and arches, except the installation time is likely to be several days (to place the substrate in the culvert) and a full channel diversion is required. Channel construction – as for bridges, but it mostly occurs inside the culvert. The new channel immediately below the culvert must be fully armoured and immovable up to the top of the material placed in the culvert (40% of the diameter for a round culvert, 20% for a pipe-arch or elliptical culvert). In my opinion that there must be NO opportunity for vertical movement of the material in the culvert, contrary to Robison (2006) – any scouring will reduce the stability of the remaining substrate and will reduce the ability of the culvert to pass fish. Downstream sedimentation after installation – as for arches. Flood water impacts – The significance of abnormally high flows can only be minimized by increasing the width of the culvert. Abnormally high flows carry the risk of scouring out some or all of the substrate in the culvert. I have observed another scouring method – winter ice can bind to the surface rocks, and then lift up and carry the rocks out of the culvert during spring run-off; this can remove the large surface rocks important for current shadows that assist fish passage. Bedload and Debris movement – bedload and debris can very easily accumulate in a culvert, and cleaning it out is difficult. Bedload may fill around the large surface rocks, reducing their effectiveness in assisting fish passage. This will also reduce culvert flow capacity and the effective width of the streambed. Therefore embedded culverts are not recommended for sites with noticeable bedload or debris movement. Beaver dams – beavers will base their dams on any structure that narrows the channel, or otherwise makes dam construction more efficient. The inlet of an embedded culvert qualifies as such a location; the interior of culverts is also sometimes used as a dam site. Embedded culverts were therefore not recommended for any sites with beaver activity. 21 3.1.3. Cost Estimates The guidance provided by Robison (2006) for calculating cost estimates is incomplete and clearly only preliminary. The guidelines do not consider paved roads, railways, public highways, multi- lane roads, road corners, extra long structures, or abnormally deep or shallow road fill depths. He did not provide any cost estimates for culvert replacements in non-fish streams or for sediment control measures. The example costs that are provided in the guidelines are significantly lower than those I am aware of from the last few years, and lower than than those from the experience of Brian Bentley, P. Eng. The cost estimates in the guidelines are focused on projects costing under $100,000; in this project a high proportion of fish passage remedial measures are likely to cost well over that amount, including over $1 million dollars. The cost estimates developed for this project are based on personal experience, logic, quotes from Armtec of Prince George for two typical open-bottom arch sizes, input from Brain Bentley, P. Eng., and a considerable amount of educated guesswork. Estimated typical costs developed for bridges, open-bottom arches, and embedded culverts are provided in the “Methods”. These “typical” costs were adjusted for the various factors that Robison did not consider. The cost estimates should only be used as “ball park” figures, for use in selecting sites for treatment based on available budgets. Once a specific site has been selected, an engineer should do a detailed site design consistent with the recommendations in this report. From that site design the engineer can do a detailed cost estimate, and an RFP issued. The costs of stream crossing structures have been rising rapidly in the last few years; if that trend continues then the estimates in this report can be expected to become increasingly outdated. 3.1.4. Prioritization The prioritization matrix developed for this project is simplistic, and preferably would have included factors such as whether there is a partial or full barrier to fish passage, the amount and quality of upstream fish habitat that will become available once the barrier is removed, and the number and identity of the fish species affected (especially bull trout). However, such data were inadequately present for the sites examined in this project, and hence these variables were not considered. In this project there are sufficiently few streams with known fish presence (S1 to S4) that required remedial action that further prioritization is not immediately required. However, once many of the “possibly fish bearing” streams (P1 to P4) have fish presence confirmed, there is likely to be a large enough number of sites requiring remedial action that further prioritization will be desirable. It is therefore desirable that for such sites the amount and quality of upstream habitat be determined, for a suggested minimum of 1 km upstream. 3.1.5. Beaver Issues A significant number of culverts were plugged, or had recently been plugged, by beaver dams. This was the largest single cause of the high number in the “roadbed or ditch washout hazard” category of Table 6. There were a few existing attempts to prevent this problem using trash racks or chicken wire placed over the culvert inlets; there were no commercial “beaver stops” (used here as a generic term, not a brand name) or other serious attempts at preventing beaver plugging without impeding fish passage. Beaver stops are usually constructed as cylindrical wire cages projecting out 2-3 metres from a culvert inlet. Some designs have a smaller inner cage enclosed in a larger outer cage. 22 I consulted with Ken Randle of West Fraser Mills (Quesnel), who has extensive experience in managing beaver plugging of culverts, and that conversation combined with my more limited experience is the basis for the following comments. Commercial “beaver stops” are not very successful because they are frequently crushed by snow and ice build-up in the winter; presumably they work in warmer climates. Ken consulted with the manufacturers and tried various solutions to this problem, but none worked well. The winter crushing occurs along both plowed and unplowed roads, but not all beaver stops are crushed. He has found that steel remesh (reinforcing mesh) used in concrete work can be used to construct beaver stops as good as or better than commercial products. They are much cheaper when made in-house and are more resistant to crushing, although they rust sooner. Beaver stops cannot be used on culverts larger than about 1600 mm, cannot be used on streams with debris or bedload movement, and always require constant monitoring and maintenance to remove debris. Bridges or large (> 3 m) open- bottom arches or (where there are no fish) culverts > 3m are the preferred option to prevent beaver problems. I suggest that, based on my observations but not literature review, a low-maintenance alternative to beaver stops is to install a 0.5 m high rock weir about 2 metres back from the crossing structure inlet without impeding fish passage, to encourage beaver dam construction away from the inlet. If the stream channel is being reconstructed during bridge or open-bottom arch construction, the surface of the new stream channel should be carried to the top of the weir, resulting in a shallow pool above the upstream end of the new channel. Beavers will usually choose to construct their dam on the top of the weir, back from the crossing structure inlet, reducing the chance that the crossing structure itself will be dammed. This effect will be enhanced if the stream channel has a measurable gradient, because beavers prefer to pond low gradient sites, although this will usually not be possible to achieve at low gradient crossings. I have made recommendations consistent with this for sites with identified beaver concerns. 23 3.2. Suggested Future Work 3.2.1. Existing Fish Inventory Data Summary and Stream Classification Compile all existing fish inventory data for the project area at a minimum, although for the entire South Peace would be desirable and only a moderate increase in work load. Interpret that data by coding all TRIM water features by fish species present or absent, known or default. See for the example for the Quesnel Forest District: http://srmapps.gov.bc.ca/appsdata/acat/html/deploy/acat_p_report_8109.html This is an essential activity to provide an accurate fish bearing status for all the “P” stream crossings that have only provisional stream classes, and a critical preliminary step prior to doing further field inventory. 3.2.2. Additional Fish and Fish Habitat Inventory Conduct fish inventories specifically designed to identify all larger watersheds (P1 to P3) as definitely fish bearing or non-fish bearing, and as many P4 to P6 watersheds as possible. Non-fish bearing results for the larger streams will usually confirm the non-fish status of smaller tributary streams, without further inventory. I recommend use of the FPC Fish Stream Identification Guidebook “Method B”, not the RISC Reconnaissance (1:20,000) Fish and Fish Habitat Inventory methods. The Fish Stream Identification Guidebook method is designed for a qualified Professional to conclusively establish fish presence/absence in a stream, and is highly time/cost efficient for that purpose. In contrast, the Reconnaissance Inventory method is designed to determine the general distribution and abundance of fish in a watershed; it does not conclusively establish fish absence from a stream, and it is very time/cost inefficient for that purpose. 3.2.3. Stream Crossing Assessment Guidelines Revise Robison (2006) based on the experience from this project. Consider formatting the guidelines into “modules” designed to address different objectives – the requirements for a single stream crossing assessment are quite different from multiple assessments in watershed-level projects such as this one. The sections on choice of appropriate treatments and cost estimates need considerably more guidance with respect to a wide range of circumstances. 3.2.4. Road Maintenance Establish a multi-road user protocol to ensure that all non-MoT road culverts are inspected, and if necessary maintained, at least once a year. CNR should have its own protocol to ensure that all their culverts, for both the railbed and access roads, are inspected and maintained at least once a year. 24
